subject: Food Science
title: The Maillard Reaction
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Maillard Reaction usable.

hook.text: The golden crust on bread, the sear on steak, the brown of roasted coffee—all come from one chemical reaction discovered in 1912.

buildup.text: The Maillard reaction occurs between amino acids and sugars when heated above 140°C.

discovery.text: It produces pyrazines (nutty, roasted), furanones (caramel), and melanoidins (brown pigments).

twist.text: The Maillard reaction doesn't occur in water (boiling maxes at 100°C). That's why boiled meat is bland but grilled meat is rich.

climax.text: Baking soda raises pH and accelerates Maillard browning. Pretzels get their deep color from a lye bath.

punchline.text: One reaction: amino acids plus sugars plus heat. It created bread crust, coffee flavor.

quiz.question: Why doesn't the Maillard reaction occur in boiling water?
options: Boiling water maxes at 100°C—Maillard requires above 140°C
